data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["In chess, the heuristic often relies on statistical patterns of human play (inductive), whereas Popper insists on logical severity.","A firebreak is a physical barrier, while corroboration is an informational status.","Scientists often act as if the theory is true (betting lives/money), unlike a chess player who knows the heuristic might fail against a novel strategy."],"overturn_conditions":["If it is shown that 'severity' cannot be assessed without assuming the uniformity of natural laws.","If acting on a theory logically entails believing it will succeed in the immediate future."],"shared_structure":["Selection of an option based on its history of surviving stressors, not on a prediction of future safety.","The goal is to keep the system (science/forest/game) in a state where catastrophic failure can be quickly identified and contained.","Preference is procedural (maximizing information flow) rather than predictive (maximizing win/survival probability)."],"source_memory_refs":["chess-grandmaster-heuristic","firebreak-forestry-strategy"],"transfer_claims":["Just as a forester chooses the oldest burn scar for a new firebreak not because it won't burn again, but because it has proven most resistant so far, scientists choose corroborated theories to maximize the informational yield of the next test.","The rationality lies in the maintenance of the critical process, not in the outcome of the specific instance."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a non-inductive methodological rule to maximize the severity of future tests; accepting this costs us the assurance that our chosen theory is likely true or will survive, restricting rationality to the procedural virtue of keeping error-elimination active.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'severity' implicitly assumes that nature is uniform enough for past harsh tests to matter for future ones, the distinction collapses into hidden induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If scientists actually act on the belief that corroborated theories will work (pragmatic success), then Popper's reconstruction fails to describe actual rational agency.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the choice of which theory to test next cannot be made without assigning some likelihood of failure, the 'non-inductive' label is merely semantic.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'justification' (which Popper rejects) and 'critical preference.' By defining corroboration as a report of past test severity rather than a probability metric, the preference for the best-corroborated theory becomes a strategic choice to subject the most vulnerable (and thus most informative) survivor to the next attempt at falsification. This avoids induction because it makes no claim about the future reliability of the theory, only about the current optimality of the testing situation.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
